claims.text: Tailored thermo-mechanical processing that produces refined grains and uniformly distributed nanoscale precipitates will concurrently improve strength, ductility, Young’s modulus, and fracture resistance relative to conventional processing.
Conventionally as-cast or homogenized high-entropy alloys exhibit coarse grains and a homogeneous single-phase microstructure.
Controlled plastic deformation followed by optimized annealing or aging can induce grain refinement and nanoscale precipitate formation.
A narrow processing window is required to obtain uniformly distributed nanoscale precipitates without coarsening.
The proposed benefits depend on using alloy compositions capable of forming stable precipitates.
The processing route will produce reduced grain size together with uniformly dispersed nanoscale precipitates.
Uniformly dispersed nanoscale precipitates act as barriers to dislocation movement.
Uniformly dispersed nanoscale precipitates act as barriers to crack propagation.
Precipitate-induced impediment of dislocation motion increases strength.
Precipitate-induced impediment of dislocation motion increases effective Young’s modulus.
Refined grains and precipitate interfaces facilitate plasticity and thereby increase ductility.
Refined grains and precipitate interfaces promote crack deflection and thereby increase fracture resistance.
The treated alloy will show statistically significant improvements in all measured key mechanical properties relative to the conventional baseline.
Enhancements reported in the literature are generally on the order of 10–30%.
Conventionally processed high-entropy alloys typically have moderate strength and toughness because of their coarse, homogeneous microstructure.
The hypothesis is most likely to hold in alloys capable of forming coherent or semi-coherent nanoscale precipitates.
Limited precipitate stability or formation of coarser phases may prevent the intended multifunctional improvements.
The magnitude and reproducibility of the improvements depend on processing precision and alloy chemistry.

contradictions.description: The central prediction requires concurrent statistically significant improvement in all key properties, whereas the falsification rule requires less than a 10% increase in multiple properties. Thus, a statistically significant improvement below 10% in all properties could both satisfy the qualitative hypothesis and trigger its stated falsification rule; conversely, failure of only one property could contradict the all-properties claim without necessarily meeting the rule.
